statement: Computed here (src/physics/control.ts): the best linear (matched-filter) estimate of one patch’s activity from N electrodes spread evenly over the four-shell sphere of section 3, against the brain’s background (independent radial dipoles over the cortex sphere, seen through the same head) and white electrode noise, has SNR² = tᵀC⁻¹t. It is solved exactly in electrode space up to 128 electrodes and per spherical-harmonic degree above that, the degrees finer than the array resolves (l > √N − 1) counted as noise; the two agree within 1% at 128 to 256 electrodes. With 1 µV of electrode noise and 10 µV of background, a 10 nA·m patch of 10 mm radius reaches 0.43 with 64 electrodes, 0.69 with 256 and 0.90 with 100,000, against 4.9, 10 and 197 with the electrode noise alone.
sources: Kay SM (1998). Fundamentals of Statistical Signal Processing, Volume II: Detection Theory. Prentice Hall.
de Munck JC, Vijn PCM, Lopes da Silva FH (1992). A random dipole model for spontaneous brain activity. IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering 39(8):791–804. doi:10.1109/10.148387
note_for_auditor: The numbers are computed by the site’s own code (not checkable against a source). Check that the method is standard: matched-filter SNR² = tᵀC⁻¹t for a known pattern t in Gaussian noise of covariance C (Kay 1998), N samples on a sphere resolving spherical-harmonic degrees up to about √N − 1 because there are (L+1)² coefficients up to degree L, and a background of independent random dipoles (de Munck et al. 1992). Say whether the cited sources support what is attributed to them.

statement: Computed here: with the whole scalp potential known exactly, the head’s transfer cancels, because the patch and the background pass through the same head, and the SNR reaches a ceiling set by the background sources under the patch’s own footprint, SNR² = Q² Σ (2l+1) g_l² / β (g_l the disc’s smoothing per degree, β the background density). For 10 nA·m over a 10 mm radius against 10 µV of background the ceiling is 0.99, and halving the radius doubles it. Grover & Venkatesh argue that when brain noise dominates, the sensor count at which localization stops improving could be quite high; in this model the approach to the ceiling is slow when the electrode noise is low.
sources: Grover P, Venkatesh P (2017). An information-theoretic view of EEG sensing. Proceedings of the IEEE 105(2):367–384. doi:10.1109/JPROC.2016.2615179
note_for_auditor: Derived. If the patch and the background reach the scalp through the same per-degree transfer c_l, the per-degree SNR² is v_l²/C_l with v_l ∝ Q c_l g_l and C_l ∝ β c_l², so c_l cancels; check this reasoning and whether Grover & Venkatesh (2017) say what is attributed to them about brain noise and the number of sensors.

statement: Evoked responses: a P300 speller gained nothing significant from 13 electrodes added to a set of 6, and more than 8 electrodes gave small gains or losses depending on the classifier; flicker-frequency decoding saturated with 9 to 32 parieto-occipital electrodes once more than 0.2 s of data was used, while decoding where the user fixated kept gaining up to 66; over occipital cortex, four-class visual-category decoding rose from 57% with about 9 electrodes to 73% with 464 (4 subjects); source-localization error fell from 27 mm with 32 channels to 21, 20 and 18 mm with 64, 128 and 256, the last step called modest.
sources: Krusienski DJ, Sellers EW, McFarland DJ, Vaughan TM, Wolpaw JR (2008). Toward enhanced P300 speller performance. Journal of Neuroscience Methods 167(1):15–21. doi:10.1016/j.jneumeth.2007.07.017

statement: Motor-imagery decoders peak with 10 to 50 well-placed channels: in 80 users recorded with 119 channels the best of 13 fixed montages had 48 channels, and montages of 8 to 32 were not significantly worse when few training trials were available; on a 118-channel dataset 22.6 selected channels scored 82.3% against 73.6% with all 118; predicted error stayed near 3% from 52 channels down to about 14; a review puts the number that can be dropped to without significant loss at 10 to 20.
sources: Sannelli C, Dickhaus T, Halder S, Hammer EM, Müller K-R, Blankertz B (2010). On optimal channel configurations for SMR-based brain–computer interfaces. Brain Topography 23(2):186–193. doi:10.1007/s10548-010-0135-0

statement: A decoder that learns its spatial weights needs the channel covariance, which is hard to estimate in high-dimensional sensor spaces, so shrinkage regularisation is used; for an adaptive array that estimates the covariance from K independent samples of N channels, the expected output SNR relative to the optimum is (K + 2 − N)/(K + 1), so about 2N samples are needed to come within a factor of two (3 dB). In a band B hertz wide independent samples arrive at 2B per second, so 2N samples take N/B seconds.
sources: Blankertz B, Lemm S, Treder M, Haufe S, Müller K-R (2011). Single-trial analysis and classification of ERP components: a tutorial. NeuroImage 56(2):814–825. doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2010.06.048

Shannon CE (1949). Communication in the presence of noise. Proceedings of the IRE 37(1):10–21. doi:10.1109/JRPROC.1949.232969
note_for_auditor: Check the Reed–Mallett–Brennan result (mean normalised output SNR (K + 2 − N)/(K + 1) for K samples and N array elements; K ≈ 2N for a 3 dB loss), the Blankertz 2011 statement about covariance estimation and shrinkage, and that 2B independent samples per second for a band B wide is Shannon 1949.

statement: Electrode counts of real systems: the International 10–20 system places 19 electrodes on the scalp (21 with two ear references); research caps go up to 256 electrodes (BioSemi 16 to 256; EGI nets 32 to 256), commercial high-density systems mostly using 160 to 256 channels; ultra-high-density grids reach 1,024 channels 8.6 mm apart; consumer headsets use 1 to 14.
